Code Defect: Before removing an export from a shared infrastructure module (e.g., `preview/globals`, `manager/globals`, or any `definitions`/`globals` barrel), verify the export is not imported anywhere in the monorepo—including builder packages and other lib packages—and confirm with teammates that no in-progress work depends on it; if uncertain, keep the export and add a TODO comment rather than deleting it.

When migrating addon `package.json` entries from `peerDependencies` to `devDependencies`, audit each package's actual import usage in the addon's source files before including it as a devDependency; do not mechanically carry over every previous peer dep—remove packages (e.g., `react-dom`) that are not directly imported by the addon's own source.
Avoid using CSS properties or values with limited browser support (e.g., `white-space: balance`) in styled components; prefer well-supported alternatives (e.g., `white-space: normal`) instead.

Remove all debugging artifacts before merging: no `console.log`/`console.warn`/`console.error` statements, no commented-out debug blocks, and no active early-return patterns annotated with TODO/DO-NOT-MERGE comments. In server-side Node.js code under `code/{core,lib,addons,builders,frameworks,presets,renderers}/**`, use `logger` from `storybook/internal/node-logger` for all diagnostic logging instead of `console.*`. Direct `console.*` usage in renderer or utility code leaks internal paths and violates the project's logging conventions.

Do not merge code with unresolved TODO or FIXME comments for functionality intended to be part of the same change; conversely, remove any FIXME/TODO comments whose described issue has already been resolved by the PR—leftover resolved-issue annotations are misleading. Either resolve the TODO, convert it to a tracked issue, or delete it if already addressed. When writing TODO comments, make them actionable: briefly describe what needs to be done and/or include a link to a tracking issue (e.g., `// TODO: cover edge-case X, see #1234`). Do not use personal name callouts such as `// TODO: <Name> figure this out`.

Avoid bypassing TypeScript's type system via `as any` casts, `: any` annotations on exports, unverified `as SomeType` assertions, non-null assertions (`!`) on optional properties, or `@ts-expect-error` suppressions. Instead, fix the underlying type definitions to accurately reflect runtime values, use typed type-guard functions to narrow discriminated unions, provide explicit generic parameters, add runtime structural guards (e.g., `'prop' in obj` plus `Array.isArray()`), or supply explicit fallbacks (e.g., `value.type ?? 'other'`) for optional fields. A `@ts-expect-error`, `!`, or `: any` is often a signal that the type definitions need correction, not that the error should be silenced.
Do not add defensive optional chaining (e.g., `prop?.method()`) on props that are typed as required and non-nullable; unnecessary guards add noise and can mask genuine type mismatches.

When a preset hook's return type doesn't match the expected signature from `PresetProperty<T>`, fix the type definition of `PresetProperty<T>` rather than casting the return value to `never` at the call site. Casting `as never` tells TypeScript the value is impossible, silently suppressing type errors and masking the real mismatch.

When forwarding any optional property from `options.angularBuilderOptions` into `builderOptions` in `framework-preset-angular-cli.ts`, always guard the assignment with an `!== undefined` check (e.g., `if (options.angularBuilderOptions?.prop !== undefined) { builderOptions.prop = options.angularBuilderOptions.prop; }`). An unconditional optional-chain assignment will overwrite an already-merged default with `undefined` whenever the caller omits that option.

In documentation code examples (e.g., package.json script blocks, config file snippets, CSS/JSX/MDX), verify that all entries are syntactically complete, unique, and technically correct: no duplicate keys or imports, no incomplete template tokens (e.g., `<project-name` missing its closing `>`), CSS numeric values must include units (e.g., `min-height: 40px` not `min-height: 40`), code blocks must be free of stray or extraneous characters (e.g., trailing semicolons after JSX/MDX closing tags, duplicate keywords like `from  from`), all imports must be used, and API calls must use correct option names (e.g., Testing Library's `getByRole` accepts `name`, not `text`, for accessible name filtering).

Before merging MDX documentation that uses custom JSX components or references static asset paths (e.g., icon image URLs), confirm the components are implemented/exported and the asset files exist in the repository or are served by the build pipeline. Missing components silently break rendering; missing assets should be added or paths corrected consistently across all pages.

When writing a test for a concurrency/race-condition fix, ensure the test would actually fail without the fix: (1) wrap the promise under test to track a boolean `resolved` flag, (2) assert `expect(resolved).toBe(false)` after a short `setTimeout` wait but *before* releasing any blocking gate, and (3) verify that mock stubs don't inadvertently allow the awaited operation to complete early.

When calling functions that search for a descendant and may legitimately return `null`/`undefined` (e.g., `findLeafEntry` when all children are filtered out), always capture the return value and guard with a truthiness check before passing it to consumers; silently no-op when nothing is found rather than risking a runtime error.

When updating MIGRATION.md with TypeScript configuration guidance, accurately state which `moduleResolution` modes (e.g., `bundler`, `nodenext`) reject extensionless imports and specify the exact setting required (e.g., `allowImportingTsExtensions`). Do not imply extensionless imports 'continue to work' without qualifying which tsconfig resolver supports them.

When a wrapper function or utility re-exposes a generic type parameter that corresponds to a specific third-party interface (e.g., Vue's `App<HostElement>`), match that interface's own default type exactly rather than substituting a seemingly stricter alternative; diverging from upstream defaults (e.g., replacing `= any` with `= Element`) can cause type incompatibilities for callers who rely on the upstream contract.

When documentation prose names a specific version of an external tool and links to that tool's versioned documentation site, confirm that the URL's version identifier matches the version stated in the text (e.g., a reference to 'Vite 5' must link to v5.vite.dev, not v6.vite.dev).

Code examples that demonstrate package imports should use the canonical import path given in the upstream library's official documentation; do not add explicit file extensions to import specifiers when the official docs omit them (e.g., `require('next/jest')` is preferred over `require('next/jest.js')`).

When narrowing a discriminated-union variant (e.g., `TSType`) by its `name` string, also investigate whether a structural property unique to that variant (e.g., the presence or absence of `raw`, or the shape of `value`) can serve as a more robust discriminant; verify that the chosen structural property is consistent across all runtime inputs before relying on it as a type guard.

When an array property is tightened from optional (`prop?: T[]`) to required (`prop: T[]`), confirm that all runtime code paths that construct or pass that object guarantee the property is present before calling array methods (`.filter()`, `.map()`, etc.) directly on it without optional chaining.

When a React component combines controlled state (`useState`) with a native `<details>` element, ensure the `<details>` is kept in sync via an `onToggle` handler (e.g., `onToggle={(e) => setState(e.currentTarget.open)}`). Relying solely on a React `onClick` to toggle state can cause desync when assistive technologies or browser features toggle the native `<details>` element outside React's event system.

Do not remove explicit `role="button"` from styled `<summary>` elements used as interactive toggles. Although `<summary>` has an implicit ARIA button role per spec, some browsers do not expose it to assistive technologies; the explicit attribute is required for consistent cross-browser AT support.

Storybook story files for interactive components (e.g., popovers, tooltips, expandable sections) must include a `play` function that programmatically exercises the interaction (opens the popover, expands the section, etc.), so the open/expanded state is captured in visual regression tests. Where both a minimal-content and a long/complex-content story variant exist, both should have play functions. When querying by accessible name, use partial or regex matching when the name can change based on story globals or component state (e.g., locked vs. unlocked). Guard against clicking a disabled element by checking its `disabled` attribute first and early-returning if true.

When using the `in` operator to duck-type a property, first verify the value is a non-null object (`value !== null && typeof value === 'object'`) since `in` throws a TypeError on primitives and `null`. Then also validate the property's runtime type—for example, add `Array.isArray(obj.prop)` before calling array methods such as `.length` or iterating, rather than relying on property existence alone.

When submitting a dependency version bump in `package.json` (and the accompanying lockfile update), verify that the target version actually exists on the npm registry before opening the PR (e.g., run `npm view <package> versions` or check the registry page); specifying a non-existent version will cause install and CI package-resolution to fail.

In `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/stories.ts`, whenever a defensive existence check is added or changed in one index-mutation function, audit all sibling functions (e.g., both `updateStory` and `updateDocs`) to ensure the same `if (index && index[id])` / `if (filteredIndex && filteredIndex[id])` guards are applied consistently in both the no-ref and ref branches before any mutation.

Changes to index-mutation functions in `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/stories.ts` (such as `updateStory` or `updateDocs`) must be tested for HMR regressions—verify that editing a story or docs entry still updates live in the Storybook UI without requiring a full page reload.

When augmenting a third-party TypeScript module's interface (e.g., augmenting `@emotion/react`'s `Theme` interface), always use `declare module 'the-third-party-package' { export interface Theme ... }` paired with a side-effect import of that package—never `declare module '.'`. A `declare module '.'` augmentation creates a new, local interface that does not merge with the third-party package's original interface; any code that imports `Theme` directly from the third-party package bypasses the augmentation entirely.

When reading a file at runtime, always wrap the read in a try/catch and return a sensible default on failure—even when preceded by an `existsSync` guard, since the file can be removed, become unreadable (EACCES), or turn out to be a directory (EISDIR) between the existence check and the read (TOCTOU race). On error, skip the candidate and continue rather than letting the exception propagate; this matches the defensive error-handling patterns established elsewhere in the codebase.

Choose `??` vs. `||` based on which falsy values should trigger the fallback: use `??` when `0`, `''`, or `false` are legitimate values (it only triggers on `null`/`undefined`); use `||` when the variable defaults to `''` (empty string) and the empty string should also trigger the fallback. For example, `detectIndent(content).indent ?? 2` preserves a valid zero-width indent, whereas `someString || 'default'` correctly replaces an empty string.

When adding a new npm package import inside a monorepo workspace, verify that the package is declared in the `dependencies` (or `devDependencies`) of the specific workspace `package.json` that contains the importing file, not only at the repository root.

When a type needs to carry symbol-keyed metadata alongside strongly-typed string keys (e.g., extending a TypeFest-based type with internal Symbol metadata), use a symbol-only index signature `{ [k: symbol]: unknown }` rather than `Record<string | symbol, any>`. The latter widens all string-keyed properties to `any`, defeating the original type's guarantees.

Unit tests must import and directly invoke the real exported function under test rather than inlining equivalent logic inside the test body. Duplicating the implementation within the test means a regression in production code won't be detected—the test passes against its own copy of the logic. Ensure the function is exported from its module so the test can call and verify actual behavior.

When code in Storybook's Next.js framework packages (e.g., under `code/frameworks/nextjs/` or `code/frameworks/nextjs-vite/`) needs to import Next.js functionality—including in mock/export files and routing providers—use the public Next.js package entrypoints (e.g., `next/headers`, `next/navigation`, `next/router`) rather than internal `next/dist/*` paths. The `next/dist/*` paths are undocumented implementation details with no stability guarantees and can change across Next.js versions.

When story parameters are attached via the detached `StoryExport.parameters = { ... }` pattern (rather than inline inside the story object), verify that the variable name used in the assignment exactly matches the story export it is intended to configure—copy-paste errors can silently apply parameters to the wrong story while leaving the intended story unconfigured. This is especially common when converting stories from the legacy function-export style to CSF3 object style.

When calling `process.exit()` on an error path (e.g., invalid user input, argument validation failure), always use a non-zero exit code such as `process.exit(1)`; using `process.exit(0)` on an error path incorrectly signals success to the calling shell or CI system.

When validating user-supplied arguments against a known list with a fuzzy-match/suggestion helper, treat every unrecognised argument as an error unconditionally—set the error flag and emit a descriptive error message even when the helper returns no close-match suggestion, rather than silently ignoring arguments for which no match is found.

When building URL query strings or path segments manually, prefer native `URLSearchParams` (which handles encoding automatically) over hand-rolled string concatenation; if manual construction is unavoidable, URL-encode every variable key and value with `encodeURIComponent` to prevent broken URLs from special characters.

Shortcut case handlers in `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/shortcuts.ts` that invoke story-dependent APIs (e.g., `fullAPI.getStoryHrefs`) must guard against `storyId` being `undefined` (possible on non-story pages such as About or Settings) with an explicit `if (!storyId) { break; }` before executing the action.

After verifying that a composed-ref entry (`refs[refId]`) exists, also check that `refs[refId].url` is a non-empty string before concatenating it to form a preview URL; skipping this check silently produces a URL like `'undefined/iframe.html'`.

Mock objects in `.stories.tsx` context fixtures must exactly match the actual API's property names and values—including correct key names (e.g., `managerHref`/`previewHref`, not `manager`/`preview`) and correct shortcut key casing—because mismatches cause stories and story-based tests to fail silently without type errors.

When splitting serialized `key:value` pairs (such as Storybook args or globals) with `.split(':')`, always pass a limit of `2` (i.e., `.split(':', 2)`) so that values which themselves contain colons (e.g., `theme:dark:blue` or `url:https://…`) are preserved in full rather than silently truncated.

When mocking Next.js (or other versioned framework) internal modules that were restructured between major versions, use dynamic `import()` wrapped in try/catch—following the pattern used in the webpack framework adapter—so the mock works across all supported framework versions rather than hard-coding a static import that fails in older versions.

When writing inline comments or JSDoc that reference environment variable names, verify that each name in the prose exactly matches the variable used in the surrounding code—the compiler will not catch a mismatch between a name in a comment and the actual variable (e.g., writing `BUILD_MODE` when the code uses `BUILD_TARGET`).

When looking up a value from a `Record`/map by a dynamic key (e.g., `filters[someKey].property`), always use optional chaining (`?.`) so that an unexpected or absent key does not throw at runtime; provide an explicit fallback value rather than relying on the key always being present.

When an effect hook injects a DOM element with a known ID via `insertAdjacentHTML` or similar, first check `document.getElementById(id)` and skip insertion if the element already exists, preventing duplicates when multiple component instances mount. In the corresponding cleanup, retrieve the element with `getElementById` and guard the removal with an existence check (e.g., `element?.parentNode?.removeChild(element)`) rather than a non-null assertion, so the cleanup does not throw if the element was already removed by other code.

When a helper called inside a `useEffect` body returns a cleanup/teardown function, capture that return value and invoke it inside the `useEffect`'s own cleanup callback; silently discarding it means teardown logic (e.g., restoring a DOM style property) never runs when the effect re-fires or the component unmounts.

Do not parse a CSS `filter` property value by splitting on whitespace—filter functions such as `drop-shadow(2px 2px 4px black)` contain spaces within their arguments and will be fragmented incorrectly. Instead, save the entire original filter string before modification and restore it verbatim in cleanup, or use a regex that matches complete filter function tokens.

TypeScript triple-slash directives (`/// <reference types="..." />`) must not be followed by a trailing semicolon; the semicolon causes TypeScript to treat the line as an ordinary comment rather than a directive.

When writing a dynamic `import()` expression for a third-party package, verify whether the target symbol is a default export or a named export before deciding on import syntax. CommonJS-compiled packages frequently expose their main class only as a default export; destructuring `{ SymbolName }` from such a module yields `undefined` at runtime. If the package uses a default export, access it as `(await import('pkg')).default`.

Before adding `import type { SomeName }` from a package (external or internal), confirm that `SomeName` is actually present in that package's published type declarations or exports. For external packages, check `.d.ts` files or re-exports. For internal renderer types (e.g., a framework type alias in a renderer's `types.ts`), verify the type is defined and exported. Before importing from a framework package's subpath (e.g., `@storybook/vue3-vite/node`), verify the type is actually exported from that entry point. For any import (type or runtime) from a package subpath (e.g., `package/subpath`), verify the subpath is declared in the package's `exports` field; an undeclared subpath causes a runtime module-resolution failure regardless of whether TypeScript compiles cleanly. If the type does not exist, define it locally—for example via `ConstructorParameters<typeof ThePlugin>[0]` or a hand-written interface—or reuse an existing type rather than importing a non-existent named type.

When writing GitHub Actions conditions to detect or skip fork PRs, use `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.fork != true` rather than comparing `github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository`. The `full_name` comparison can silently misbehave when `head.repo` is null (e.g., the originating fork was later deleted), while the boolean `fork` property is the purpose-built, null-safe alternative. This pattern is already established in `trigger-circle-ci-workflow.yml` and should be used consistently across all workflow files.
Unit tests for URL-building functions must include cases for special characters in parameter values (e.g., `=`, `&`, `;`, `:` within a value) to verify that encoding is applied correctly end-to-end.

Do not use `rel="canonical"` on `<a>` elements—the canonical link type is only valid on `<link>` tags in the document `<head>` for SEO canonicalization. On anchor tags, omit `rel` entirely for internal navigation links and use `rel="noreferrer"` only for external links that open in a new tab.

Components that render `href` attributes derived from current navigation state (e.g., the active settings-tab path in the sidebar Menu) must subscribe to routing state changes so the `href` value stays accurate throughout the session. A static `href` computed at initial render silently becomes stale after navigation and can mislead users and crawlers.

Avoid redeclaring, shadowing, or confusingly naming a local variable the same as an imported symbol or a binding already in scope from an enclosing destructuring. Before introducing a new `const`, verify no binding with the same name exists in the current or outer scope; before returning an expression, verify each identifier resolves to the intended binding. This is a recurring pitfall in `manager-api` modules that destructure `store.getState()`.

When implementing paired sibling-navigation helpers in `manager-api/modules/stories.ts` (e.g., `findSiblingComponent` and `findSiblingStory`), both helpers must derive the active ref context from the same source. Prefer reading `refId` from the fully resolved story/item object (e.g., `story.refId`) rather than reading it directly from raw state, so both helpers behave consistently when navigating across refs.

When reading a feature flag from `global.FEATURES` inside manager components (e.g., `Sidebar.tsx`, `GuidePage.tsx`), always use optional chaining together with a `!== false` guard—`global.FEATURES?.flagName !== false`—so that the flag defaults to its enabled state (`true`) when `FEATURES` is undefined, which can occur in tests and stories.

Preset functions that invoke external analysis utilities (e.g., docgen extraction, file reads) and utilities that parse stringified function source (e.g., regex-based source parsing in `mount-utils.ts`) must wrap those calls in `try/catch` and return a safe fallback (e.g., `null`) on failure so that exceptions do not propagate and crash preset loading or story rendering.

Always use `getProjectRoot()` from `storybook/internal/common` when computing paths relative to the project root; do not use `process.cwd()`, which may differ from the project root when the Node process is launched from a subdirectory.

When a result object uses a boolean `success` discriminator alongside optional fields, model it as a proper TypeScript discriminated union (`{ success: true; fieldA: string } | { success: false; error?: string }`) so the compiler narrows required fields within branches and non-null assertions are unnecessary.

When generating mock or dummy values for compound types (arrays, tuples), iterate over each element's `SBType` and call the value generator recursively rather than hardcoding a single scalar for all elements; e.g., a `[number, string]` tuple should produce `[42, '']`, not `['mock string', 'mock string']`.

When a type-name allowlist guards renderer-specific handling at one layer of the type-mapping pipeline (e.g., array-element processing in `extractDocgenInfo`), keep it in sync with all type-name mappings defined at higher or peer layers; any name handled by the top-level mapping (e.g., `JSX.Element`, `ComponentType`) must also appear in downstream allowlists that gate element-level handling.

When reading ArgType metadata such as the `required` flag, access it from the `ArgType` entry itself (e.g., `argType.required`), not from the nested `SBType` object; `SBType` carries no `required` field, so reading from there will always yield `undefined`.

When writing functions that sanitize or generate JavaScript identifier names by stripping invalid characters (e.g., `sanitizeIdentifier` in `csf-tools/vitest-plugin/component-transformer.ts`), also verify that the resulting string does not start with a digit—JS identifiers cannot begin with `[0-9]`. If the sanitized value starts with a digit, prefix it with `_` (or another safe character) before returning it, in addition to any existing empty-string fallback.

In test files, the module path passed to `vi.mock()` must exactly match the module path used in `import` statements in the file under test; a mismatch silently leaves the real implementation in place and causes tests to call production code instead of the mock.

Catch blocks must not silently swallow errors; never use empty `catch {}` blocks, including in test lifecycle hooks (e.g., Storybook `afterEach` hooks in `test-annotations.ts`). Even for non-critical or best-effort code paths, log the caught error at minimum at debug level (using `logger.debug` from `storybook/internal/node-logger` on the server side) or forward it to a reporting API (e.g., `reporting.addReport()`) before continuing or returning, so failures remain visible during troubleshooting. In build scripts and prebuild files specifically, catch blocks must rethrow the error rather than only logging it; swallowing errors in build pipelines discards the stack trace and makes root causes invisible to CI and local debugging.

All return paths of a function must return a consistent type; an early-exit guard that returns `undefined` (or nothing) when every other path returns a typed value is a bug—return the same type on all branches.
Guard-and-early-return checks must be placed before the work they are meant to skip; do not call an expensive function and then check afterward whether you should have called it.
Use `import { join } from 'path'` (platform-aware) rather than `import { join } from 'path/posix'` for paths passed to file-system operations or external processes, to avoid breakage on Windows.
When a computed value (such as an elapsed duration) is calculated before a conditional return, use that computed value in the returned payload rather than a hardcoded fallback (e.g., `0`).

External sub-process invocations (e.g., spawning `vitest` or other CLI tools via `executeCommand`) must be bounded by a timeout; use `Promise.race` with a rejection timer or a timeout option on the execution API to prevent indefinite hanging.

Always wrap `JSON.parse` calls that parse data from external sources (files, process output, network responses) in a try-catch block, and return a descriptive error object on parse failure rather than letting the exception propagate as an unhandled error.
Remove duplicate entries from exported array constants; duplicates waste memory, can produce unexpected behaviour in callers that iterate or check membership, and indicate a copy-paste mistake.

When a `useEffect` registers window-level event listeners (mousemove, mouseup, etc.) inside a nested callback (e.g., an onStart handler spawned from a mousedown), the effect's cleanup function must also remove those nested window listeners. Only cleaning up the directly-registered listeners leaves orphaned handlers if the component unmounts mid-interaction.

Utility functions that cycle or index into a collection must handle the empty-collection edge case explicitly. If the stated return type is non-nullable (e.g., `string`) but `Object.keys(map).length` could be 0, add an early guard that returns a safe sentinel or throws a descriptive error rather than silently returning `undefined`.

Do not use `.replace('px', '')` to extract numeric values from CSS dimension strings. This silently produces wrong results for non-pixel units (`%`, `em`, `rem`, `vw`, `vh`). Use `parseFloat()` or a regex that strips any trailing unit characters (e.g., `/[a-z%]+$/i`) so all unit types are handled correctly.

When renaming a DOM element's `id` (or the selector used to query it), search the entire codebase for every consumer of the old ID—`querySelector`/`querySelectorAll` calls, `href` skip-link anchors, `aria-controls`/`aria-labelledby` attributes, and tests—and update them all in the same commit. Partial migrations silently break features such as skip navigation.

Every `<input>` element must have an associated `<label>` element linked via a stable ID. Use `useId` (e.g., from `@react-aria/utils`) to generate a unique ID and pass it to both the `htmlFor` attribute of the label and the `id` attribute of the input. Unlabeled inputs are a WCAG 2.1 Level A violation and will be flagged by accessibility audits.

When a toolbar or canvas control's state is externally locked (e.g., overridden by story globals or parameters), every interactive control that would mutate that state—buttons, text inputs, select dropdowns—must be visually disabled (`disabled` attribute or `aria-disabled`) and reject interaction. A control that accepts input but silently does nothing is both a misleading UX and an accessibility failure.

When a preset-selection dropdown coexists with freeform value inputs (e.g., a viewport picker alongside width/height fields), the dropdown must expose a distinct 'Custom' or equivalent state that activates whenever the user overrides the preset values. Without it, selecting or opening the dropdown can silently discard the user's custom values.

Toolbar addons and canvas-level UI that are only meaningful in story mode must gate their rendering on `viewMode`. Rendering addon controls in docs mode (or other non-story contexts) where they have no effect produces confusing, non-functional UI.

When writing a regex to validate that a parsed token is a JavaScript identifier, use a complete pattern that constrains every character—e.g., `/^[a-z_$][0-9a-z_$]*$/i`—rather than a partial check that only inspects the first and last characters; partial checks silently allow strings like `foo-bar` or `a#b` to pass.

Before inserting any variable into a `new RegExp(...)` constructor, escape all regex metacharacters in the variable first (e.g., `v.replace(/[.*+?^${}()|[\]\\]/g, '\\$&')`), even when the variable is derived from a trusted internal source such as stringified function source; skipping this step risks regex injection, parse errors, and ReDoS exposure.

When using a regex pattern like `{([^}]+)}` to capture content inside braces, be aware that it will prematurely terminate at the first `}` when the content itself contains nested braces (e.g., default values such as `{ a = { nested: true } }`); either use a balanced-brace algorithm, restrict usage to contexts where nesting is impossible, or add a JSDoc/inline comment explicitly documenting the known limitation.

When extracting the body of a stringified function, match from the first `{` to the *last* `}` using a greedy pattern such as `/^[^(]*\([^)]*\)[^{]*\{([\s\S]*)\}\s*$/`; a pattern that terminates at the first `}` will silently truncate the body of any function whose body contains nested `{}` blocks (object literals, control-flow statements, etc.).

Avoid `forEach(async (item) => { ... })` when sequential execution is intended; this pattern fires all iterations concurrently and silently discards the returned Promises, causing interleaved output and no ordering or error-propagation guarantees. Use `for (const item of list) { await ... }` instead, and ensure any accompanying code comments accurately reflect whether execution is sequential or parallel.

When assigning to a nested property on an externally-sourced options or config object (e.g., `programmaticOptions.env.bugfixes = true`), always guard that the intermediate object exists before assigning into it—e.g., `obj.prop = obj.prop || {};`—rather than assuming the caller populated it. Check how the same file already handles analogous nested-property access and follow the same defensive pattern for consistency.

When a test file imports a module that the corresponding production/runtime code also imports, ensure both use the same import form (default import vs. named import). A mismatch can silently mask ESM/CJS export incompatibilities that only surface in production, and makes the test a poor proxy for real-world behavior.

Switch `case` clauses that declare local variables (`const` or `let`) must wrap their entire body in a `{ }` block to comply with Biome's `noSwitchDeclarations` rule and prevent the variable from being accessed by other cases.

When CSS dimensions are computed using a reciprocal scale factor (e.g., `(1 / scale) * 100%` paired with `transform: scale(scale)`) or any division-based arithmetic, guard against zero, negative, and non-finite values at both the input-validation layer and defensively at the computation site (e.g., `Math.max(scale, 0.001)`) to prevent `Infinity`, `NaN`, or negative CSS values from corrupting the layout. Do not apply a numeric scale multiplier directly to percentage-unit strings—percentages are relative, not absolute; restrict numeric scaling to absolute-unit values (px, em, rem) or pass percentage units through unmodified.

When using `forwardRef<T, P>`, the generic `T` must exactly match the object returned by `useImperativeHandle`. If the ref should expose a custom interface (e.g., `{ select: () => void }`), return that interface from the factory function rather than forwarding the raw DOM element; or change the generic to the actual DOM element type if direct element access is intended.

When guarding on the result of `String.prototype.search()`, use `index >= 0` (or `index !== -1`), not `index > 0`. The value `0` is a valid match position at the start of the string, so `> 0` silently skips that case. The same applies to `indexOf()`.

Avoid `Array.prototype.findLast()` (ES2023) and `Array.prototype.at()` (ES2022) unless the project's browserslist or build pipeline explicitly targets environments that ship these methods natively. Use ES2020-compatible alternatives: `[...arr].reverse().find(pred)` instead of `arr.findLast(pred)`, and `arr[arr.length - 1]` instead of `arr.at(-1)`.

In numeric input handlers, detect `NaN` with an explicit `Number.isNaN(value)` check and early `return` rather than relying on numeric comparison operators. Because `NaN >= 0` evaluates to `false`, guards that rely on numeric comparisons silently swallow NaN without making the intent clear, leading to subtle downstream bugs.

When spawning child processes with `spawn()`, always attach both an `'error'` listener and a `'close'` listener. Without an `'error'` handler, a spawn failure (bad interpreter path, missing file, permission denied) emits an unhandled `error` event that crashes the Node process. The `'error'` handler should log via `logger.error` without rethrowing. When spawning shell scripts, use the bare interpreter name `'sh'` rather than an absolute path like `'/bin/sh'`; POSIX does not require `sh` to live in `/bin/`, and Node.js resolves bare command names through `$PATH`.

Use optional chaining (`?.`) consistently throughout a property access chain on a potentially-null value; avoid mixing `value?.prop` with `value['key']` (a non-optional bracket access) on the same nullable object—use `value?.['key']` for bracket access on nullable references.

Never call `.sort()` directly on a module-level constant array (e.g., `CATEGORIZATION_RULES.sort(...)`); this mutates the shared reference on every invocation. Pre-compute a sorted copy at module initialization (`const SORTED_RULES = [...CATEGORIZATION_RULES].sort(...)`) and reference that constant instead.

When querying child nodes to call element-only methods like `getBoundingClientRect()` or `getComputedStyle()`, use `firstElementChild` / `children` (which return only `Element` nodes) rather than `firstChild` / `childNodes`; the latter can return `Text` or `Comment` nodes, which will throw on element-specific API calls.

When checking CSS `opacity` for visibility, compare numerically (`parseFloat(style.opacity) > 0`) rather than via string equality (`style.opacity !== '0'`); browsers may return `'0.0'` or `'0.00'`, which string comparison incorrectly treats as visible.

When running multiple independent fallible async operations with `Promise.all`, wrap each item in a per-item try-catch (or use `Promise.allSettled`) so that one failing operation does not reject the entire batch and crash the caller; fall back to a safe default on individual errors.

Every value of an enum or category constant set must have an explicit handler in any switch/case or mapping lookup that processes it; do not allow defined values (including error/unknown categories) to fall through to a generic default when a specific, actionable description or behavior exists.

Captured error variables in `catch` blocks (e.g., `const errorMessage = error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error)`) must be used—either logged, included in the returned error payload, or forwarded to a reporting API. Leaving the variable unused silently discards diagnostic information.

When spawning child processes with a custom `env` object, always spread `process.env` first (`{ ...process.env, CUSTOM_VAR: value }`) to inherit `PATH`, `NODE_ENV`, and other required variables; providing only custom keys without the parent environment will break the spawned process.

React hooks (including `useRef`, `useState`, `useEffect`, and any custom hooks) must be called unconditionally at the top level of a component function, before any early returns or conditional branches. If a hook call appears after an early return, move it above that return. This is required by React's Rules of Hooks.

When changing the rendered element type of a component (e.g., `<div>` to `<nav>`, `<section>` to `<header>`), update every associated `useRef<T>` generic parameter to match the new element type (e.g., `useRef<HTMLDivElement>` → `useRef<HTMLElement>`) so the ref stays type-safe.

Before replacing a CSS-hide pattern (`display: none`, `visibility: hidden`, `hidden` attribute, or a wrapper that renders-but-conceals) with conditional mounting/unmounting, verify that the hidden component's internal state does not need to survive the hide/show cycle. Unmounting destroys state; CSS hiding preserves it.

When inserting new entries into a CLI flags array that will be passed to `executeCommand` (or a similar subprocess helper), check whether the array includes a `--` argument-separator and insert the new flags in the correct position relative to it. Flags pushed before `--` are consumed by the invoking command; flags pushed after `--` are forwarded to the subprocess. Misplacing a flag on the wrong side of the separator silently changes which process receives it.

When building a string array whose entries must match keys in a TypeScript interface or object literal (e.g., a `hardcodedShortcuts` or `fixedShortcuts` list used for filtering), verify the exact case-sensitive spelling of every entry against the target keys. A casing mismatch compiles without error but silently fails to match at runtime.

The keyboard shortcut key string rendered in the UI (e.g., `['alt', '+']`) must match the string registered with the shortcut system (e.g., `['alt', '=']`). On US keyboards `+` and `=` share a physical key but differ as string values; mismatched strings mean the visual hint describes a different key combination than the one that actually fires the action.

After calling a computation utility (e.g., `getComponentComplexity()`), validate the result with `Number.isFinite(result)` before using it in sorting, averaging, or other arithmetic; edge-case parsing errors or division by zero can produce `NaN`/`Infinity`, which corrupts downstream calculations.

When building argument arrays for subprocess or command execution (e.g., `executeCommand`, `spawn`), always push CLI flags and their values as separate array elements (e.g., `parts.push('-p', String(port))`) rather than as a single combined string (e.g., `parts.push(`-p ${port}`)``). A combined string is passed as one argument token, causing the flag to be silently ignored or misinterpreted by the target CLI.

When calling `api.setAddonShortcut`, every registration must use a unique `actionName`; reusing an existing `actionName` silently overrides the previously registered shortcut. If a logical action needs multiple keyboard shortcuts, use distinct `actionName` values (e.g., `zoomIn` and `zoomInAlt`)—each will appear as a separate entry in the keyboard shortcuts configuration table.

When changing error handling from throwing to silent skipping of non-conforming items (e.g., non-factory exports in `CsfFile.ts`), ensure tests cover all plausible shapes that could be accidentally dropped—including raw function components (`() => <Component />`) and plain story objects (`{ args: {} }`)—not just trivial helpers. Evaluate whether a `logger.warn()` should be emitted when items are silently skipped, so users receive diagnostic feedback instead of silently missing content.

When clamping a dimension against a minimum size constant while a zoom/scale factor is in play, clamp in logical (unscaled) units first and then multiply by scale: `Math.max(MIN, logicalValue) * scale`. Do not clamp after scaling (`Math.max(MIN, logicalValue * scale)`), because that applies the minimum in physical pixels—at non-1× zoom the displayed logical value will fall below the intended minimum.

When the CLI AST-transform layer (e.g., `eslintPlugin.ts`) matches a `CallExpression` by its callee identifier name, always resolve the identifier back to its `ImportDeclaration` and verify it originates from the expected source package before mutating the AST. Matching only the local binding name is insufficient—a user config may import an identically-named function from a different package, which must be left untouched.

When writing a regex to match or strip a specific literal sentinel/token string (e.g., the `$SNIP` marker from `cleanPaths` in `code/core/src/telemetry/sanitize.ts`), verify that no quantifier (`?`, `*`, `+`) inadvertently makes any character optional. For example, `/\$SNIP?/g` matches both `$SNI` and `$SNIP`; use `/\$SNIP/g` to match only the full intended token.

When reviewing changes to the component detection heuristic in `component-transformer.ts`, verify whether the logic correctly scopes what counts as a 'component' export. Flag any new code paths that risk generating tests for non-renderable exports (e.g., HOC factory functions), and ensure the inline comment noting future refinement is updated if the heuristic is tightened.

When building an absolute-positioned overlay (e.g., a suffix mask `div`) that must visually align with text inside a styled `<input>`, offset the overlay's `left` to match the input's horizontal padding as defined in the shared `Form/styles.ts`. To stay in sync without hardcoding, extract the padding value into a shared constant or CSS variable referenced by both the input style definition and the overlay.

When writing boolean conditions that combine multiple equality checks with `||`, ensure every disjunct is a complete comparison expression—`a === b || c` where `c` is a truthy variable is NOT equivalent to `a === b || a === c`. Always write out the full comparison on each side of `||` (and `&&`) to avoid silent operator-precedence bugs.

When adding non-editable informational elements (e.g., unit or suffix labels) adjacent to an `<input>`, give the element a stable `id` using `useId` from `@react-aria/utils` and link it to the input via `aria-describedby={suffixId}` so screen readers announce the supplementary context when the field receives focus.

When iterating over react-docgen `PropDescriptor` entries to extract type information, do not check only `tsType`. The `PropDescriptor` interface also has a `type` field used for JavaScript/PropTypes components; always fall back to `propInfo.type` when `propInfo.tsType` is absent so that non-TypeScript components are not silently dropped.

When selecting a component from react-docgen-typescript results by name, never use `filePath.includes(componentExportName)` substring matching—it produces false positives when one component name is a substring of another (e.g., 'Button' matches 'IconButton'). Prefer exact equality on `displayName` (and, where available, `actualName` or `exportName`). If file-path matching is genuinely required, use `path.basename(d.filePath, path.extname(d.filePath)) === componentExportName` for a strict comparison.

In preset functions that merge configuration from multiple sources (e.g., `internal_getArgTypesData`), explicitly passed options (`reactDocgen`, `reactDocgenTypescriptOptions`, etc.) must take priority over values derived from `presets.apply(...)`. Always merge with the caller's explicit values winning, so that call sites operating without a full presets chain (e.g., the vitest plugin) can still override behavior rather than having their options silently ignored.

When adding style properties to a styled component that composes multiple style functions (e.g., `styled(X)(styles, sizes, alignment, validation, { newProp })`), verify that new styles do not unconditionally override earlier prop-driven style functions. A plain object appended at the end of the composition chain wins over all preceding entries—e.g., `width: '100%'` appended after a `sizes` function will silently clobber prop-driven styles like `size='flex'`. When the new style could conflict, use a function form conditioned on the relevant prop (e.g., `({ size }) => ({ width: !size || size === '100%' ? '100%' : 'auto' })`).

When reviewing refactored conditional blocks that mutate object properties, verify that every assignment statement is properly enclosed within the intended `if`/`else` block—check brace placement and indentation carefully, particularly when the refactoring changes nesting depth. A misaligned or missing closing brace can silently cause mutations to execute unconditionally.

Storybook APIs that only exist in the Node.js build of a framework package (e.g., `defineMain`) must be imported from the `/node` subpath entry point (e.g., `import { defineMain } from '@storybook/angular/node'`), not from the package root.

In CSF Next documentation snippets: (1) access composed story args via `.input.args` (e.g., `...Primary.input.args`), not `.args`; (2) every snippet calling `preview.meta()` must export at least one story via `meta.story({...})` or include `export default meta`; (3) wrap auto-mocked modules with `mocked()` from `storybook/test` before calling `.mockReturnValue()` etc.; (4) always pass an explicit config object to `meta.story({...})`—do not call `meta.story()` with no arguments; (5) use `.extend()` to inherit from and modify an existing story; (6) import the preview module via subpath imports (e.g., `#.storybook/preview`) not file-relative paths; (7) in Vue snippets, the `render` function receives args as a direct parameter (`(args) => ({...})`), not destructured from a context object; (8) the MSW addon (`msw-storybook-addon`) does not support `definePreview()` annotations—configure it via CSF 3 / `main.js` style only.

When building a string by concatenating with an optional-chained expression (e.g., `a + b?.method()`), guard against the `undefined` case explicitly rather than relying on optional chaining alone—string concatenation will produce `'valueundefined'` if the optional chain resolves to `undefined`. Use a conditional instead, e.g., `b ? `${a}\n${b.method()}` : a`.

When guarding against absent or empty arrays before accessing array elements, avoid comparisons of the form `arr?.length < 1` or `arr?.length > 0`: when `arr` is `undefined` or `null`, optional chaining returns `undefined`, and relational comparisons with `undefined` produce `false` (NaN semantics), silently bypassing the guard. Use `!arr?.length` instead—it is correctly falsy for `undefined`, `null`, and zero-length arrays—or write an explicit `arr == null || arr.length === 0` check.

When a UI control gains a disabled or locked state, ensure ALL associated accessibility and presentation props—such as `ariaLabel`, `ariaDescription`, and `tooltip` on shared components like `Select`—are conditioned on that state consistently. Leaving any prop hardcoded to an interactive-state description while others are already conditional produces internally inconsistent accessibility information.

When writing regex patterns to detect CLI tool or package names in command strings (e.g., in `getCliIntegrationFromAncestry`), never make inter-word separators optional (use `create[\s\-]rsbuild` not `create[\s\-]?rsbuild`), and avoid `.includes()` for name detection—it produces false positives when the name appears inside a URL, file path, or install argument. Use a regex with position assertions (e.g., `/(?:^|\s)@tanstack\/start(?=\s|@|$)/i`) so the match is anchored to an actual invocation context. Test coverage must include negative cases for unseparated/concatenated variants and false-positive edge cases where the target string appears inside URLs or file paths.

In `render-components-manifest.ts`, when computing totals for any item category that can appear in multiple structural locations (e.g., attached to a parent manifest entry as well as standalone top-level entries), aggregate counts and error counts from ALL locations before constructing filter pills or badge HTML. When introducing a filter pill for a new item type, ensure: (a) the pill is always rendered whenever items of that type exist, independent of error state; and (b) the corresponding CSS `:target` filter selector reveals every instance of that type across the page.

When defining Commander.js CLI options: (1) if the option must carry a string value, declare it with angle brackets `<argName>` (required argument), not square brackets `[argName]`—with square brackets, passing the flag without a value sets the option to boolean `true`, silently bypassing downstream `typeof === 'string'` guards; (2) in `.option()` parser callbacks that accept numeric input, parse with `Number.parseInt` and validate numerically (e.g., `return parsedValue > 0 ? parsedValue : null`) rather than special-casing individual string representations of invalid values.

When an e2e test or test-infrastructure script reads a required environment variable whose absence should be a hard failure, do not suppress the TypeScript error with a non-null assertion (`!`). Instead, read the raw value and add an explicit runtime guard that throws a descriptive `Error` naming the variable, explaining why it is required, and—where a known default exists—pointing to it. This ensures CI and local-dev failures are immediately actionable rather than producing a cryptic downstream crash.

Every variant in a string-literal union type (such as `KnownAgentName` in `code/core/src/telemetry/detect-agent.ts`) must be reachable from at least one runtime code path in the same module (e.g., a corresponding detection branch in `detectExplicitAgent`). If a new variant is added to the union, the corresponding detection or handling logic must be implemented in the same PR; otherwise remove the variant until the implementation is ready.

In `config-to-csf-factory.ts`, when adding a catch-all `else if` branch to handle an edge case for a specific `configType`, scope the condition precisely using all available state—such as `exportDecls.length === 0`—to prevent the branch from firing on files that do contain export declarations (e.g., re-exports). Firing too broadly can introduce a duplicate default export or other incorrect output.

In story `play` functions and test utilities, never directly force-cast a `querySelector` result to `HTMLElement`. Instead, capture the result in a named variable, assert it is non-null with a descriptive error (e.g., `if (!el) throw new Error('#storybook-panel-root not found')`), and only then pass it to `within()` or other DOM APIs. Direct `as HTMLElement` casts mask null returns and produce confusing downstream failures.

When a function detects whether a configuration is already fully set up (e.g., to skip redundant postinstall steps), ensure it verifies ALL required components of the intended setup—not just a subset. A partial check (e.g., confirming only that the plugin is imported, without also confirming that `setupFiles` is configured) can cause setup to be skipped even when the configuration is incomplete, leaving users in a broken state.

In Vue template strings (in stories, decorators, and documentation snippets), use `v-bind` shorthand syntax (`:attr="expression"`) for dynamic HTML attribute bindings. Mustache interpolation (`{{ }}`) is only valid for text content—writing `attr={{expression}}` inside a tag will render literally as text instead of being evaluated as a binding.

In Storybook Vue decorator implementations, do not use `inject: [...]` to access values already passed as decorator context parameters (e.g., `globals`, `args`). No corresponding `provide` is called for these values, so injecting them triggers Vue 3 dev warnings ('injection not found'). Use the context parameter directly in `setup()` instead.

When typing interface fields that mirror Node.js or runtime environment properties (e.g., `stdoutIsTTY` from `process.stdout.isTTY`), match the runtime type exactly (e.g., `boolean | undefined` for `isTTY`) rather than narrowing it. Wherever such fields are consumed, handle `undefined` explicitly to avoid incorrect behavior in non-standard environments (piped output, CI, etc.).

When adding inline Vite plugin objects to `finalConfig.plugins` in `builder-vite`, annotate each object with `as PluginOption` or `satisfies PluginOption` (imported from `'vite'`) so TypeScript validates the shape. Because `builder-vite` supports Vite `^5.0.0 || ^6.0.0 || ^7.0.0`, any hook introduced in a later major (e.g., `configEnvironment` in Vite 6+) must be gated behind a runtime Vite-version check or omitted entirely; including it unconditionally causes a compile error for consumers on earlier Vite versions.

When URL normalization logic is used for comparison (e.g., `getSourceType` in `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/refs.ts`), ensure both operands canonicalize identically for all input variants—specifically that paths with and without trailing slashes produce the same normalized value before comparison. Add test cases in `code/core/src/manager-api/tests/refs.test.ts` covering trailing-slash / no-trailing-slash parity to prevent refs from being incorrectly classified as external.

When computing a directory base path by stripping a filename from a URL pathname (e.g., `managerBase`/`previewBase` in `code/core/src/manager-api/modules/url.ts`), verify the regex does not over-strip paths ending in a directory segment (e.g., `/storybook` should not reduce to `/`). Add unit tests for pathnames without file extensions and document any required trailing-slash assumption.

When loading template files as plain text at Node.js runtime (outside the esbuild pipeline), use `fs.readFile()` with `new URL(relativePath, import.meta.url)` rather than dynamic `import()`. Node.js cannot handle non-JS file extensions (`.txt`, `.ts` templates, etc.) via `import()` and throws `ERR_UNKNOWN_FILE_EXTENSION`.

When filtering entries from a `Map` where `null` encodes success and a non-null value (e.g., an `Error`) encodes failure, use a strict-null check (e.g., `map.get(key) !== null`) rather than property access on the stored value (e.g., `map.get(key)?.result`), which will always evaluate to `undefined` since the stored value is not an object with that property.

In `story-to-csf-factory.ts`, when adding AST visitors to rewrite cross-file story references, verify that every combination of import style (`namespaceStoryImports` via `import * as X` and `namedStoryImports` via `import { X }`) and usage syntax (property access `X.prop` and bare spread `...X`) is explicitly handled. A `MemberExpression` visitor alone will not catch bare-identifier spreads—add a separate `SpreadElement` visitor that checks whether the spread argument's identifier is present in `namedStoryImports` and rewrites it. Add a test case for each combination.

When refactoring a function by adding or removing parameters, audit every call site to confirm the argument list matches the updated signature exactly—extra or missing arguments will not always produce a type error if TypeScript is lenient or the file is JavaScript.

Side effects—such as emitting channel events, calling external APIs, or triggering mutations—must be placed inside `useEffect`, never inside `useMemo`. `useMemo` is strictly for computing memoized derived values; React may invoke it at arbitrary times and does not guarantee a single execution per render.

When implementing or reviewing mocks for Next.js components in `src/export-mocks/`, ensure all prop-driven behavioral modes are faithfully reproduced. For the `Link` mock specifically, when `legacyBehavior` is `true` the mock must pass navigation props through to its child element (mirroring the real Next.js `Link` behavior) rather than always rendering its own `<a>` element.

When porting or mirroring renderer public types (`Meta`, `StoryFn`, `StoryObj`) from the React renderer to another Storybook renderer, ensure all supporting utility types—including `AddMocks`, which preserves `Mock` types for args provided via `fn()` in `meta.args` instead of widening them to plain functions—are fully replicated and wired into `StoryObj`. Confirm completeness with type-level tests using `expectTypeOf` that verify mock function args retain their `Mock` type in story `play` functions.

Pin all third-party GitHub Actions to an immutable reference—a specific release tag (e.g., `@v1.2.3`) or a full commit SHA—rather than a mutable branch name such as `@master` or `@main`. Mutable refs allow upstream changes to silently alter workflow behavior and are a supply-chain security risk.

Every workflow step that runs `yarn release:publish` (or any command that internally calls `yarn npm publish`) must explicitly declare `YARN_NPM_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}` in its `env:` block. Do not rely solely on job-level `environment:` secret injection to provide npm authentication; omitting the explicit env var will cause the publish command to fail unauthenticated.

Before referencing a step's outputs with `steps.<id>.outputs.<name>`, confirm that a step with that exact `id` is defined within the same job. Referencing an undefined step ID is not a compile-time error in GitHub Actions—it silently evaluates to an empty string, producing incorrect runtime behavior. Use actionlint in CI to catch these as compile-time errors.

When constructing a `gh release create` command, pass boolean flags such as `--prerelease` or `--draft` directly on the command line rather than expanding an env variable that holds the string `'false'` as a positional argument. The GitHub CLI treats every positional argument after the tag as an asset file path to upload; passing the string `'false'` will cause the step to fail trying to open a nonexistent file.

When calling a local composite action from a GitHub Actions workflow, the `uses:` directive must point to the directory containing `action.yml` (e.g., `uses: ./.github/actions/my-action`), not to the YAML file itself (e.g., not `uses: ./.github/actions/my-action/action.yml`). GitHub Actions automatically discovers the `action.yml` or `action.yaml` inside the specified directory; including the filename in the path is invalid syntax.

In `workflow_dispatch` workflows that accept a PR number as input and check out that PR's code, add an explicit fail-fast step immediately after retrieving PR metadata that exits with a non-zero status when the PR is from a fork (`isCrossRepository == true`). This step must appear before any step that accesses secrets or publishes to a registry, because the admin-actor permission check only guards who triggers the workflow, not which code is executed.

When a workflow job checks out code from an external PR or fork (using a dynamic `repository`/`ref` in `actions/checkout`), do not reference local composite actions (`./.github/actions/…`) from that checked-out code. The action definition will resolve to the fork's copy rather than the repository's own copy. Either inline the steps or perform an additional checkout of the base repository's actions before using them.

When conditionally pushing a versioned package spec (e.g., `extraAddons.push('pkg@^4')`) onto an addons or extras array that may already contain entries from user-supplied options or earlier code paths, first check whether the array already contains any spec for the same base package by stripping version suffixes before comparing (e.g., match on `@chromatic-com/storybook` regardless of `@^4` suffix). Skipping this guard allows two conflicting version specs for the same package to coexist, leading to nondeterministic installs.

When pinning a third-party CLI scaffolding tool to a specific version in template or scaffold scripts (e.g., `npx create-next-app@16.0.1`), verify that every CLI flag used is documented for that exact pinned version. In particular, treat negated boolean flags (`--no-<flag>`) as suspect: check whether they appear in the tool's `--help` output for the pinned version before relying on them, as undocumented implicit negations can silently fail or be rejected.
Maintainability and Readability: When destructuring an array to skip leading elements, use an empty slot (e.g., `const [, value] = arr`) rather than a throwaway `_` variable. Named-but-unused `_`-prefixed bindings can trigger the project's `@typescript-eslint/naming-convention` lint rule. Default values can be applied in the same pattern (e.g., `const [, value = []] = arr`).

When migration docs or other documentation links to external code examples, consider whether to link to the final file on the default branch or to a PR diff. Link to a PR diff when the purpose is to show readers what changes to make; if so, ensure the surrounding prose makes it explicit so readers know to follow the diff pattern.

Use meaningful, descriptive `id` and `className` values on DOM elements; avoid placeholder names (e.g., `figure-out-id`) and legacy or ambiguous class names that no longer clearly describe the element's role.

Extract repeated or non-obvious magic values (pixel sizes, durations, numeric defaults) into named module-level constants or CSS variables. Reference these constants everywhere they appear—including inside callbacks and nested functions—so a single change propagates everywhere. Do not inline raw literals when a named constant already exists in the same file.

Use specific, user-facing text for initial or default UI states rather than vague placeholders; a label that clearly communicates what has not yet occurred is easier to understand at a glance than a generic 'not yet' phrase.

When using non-obvious encodings in source code (e.g., a two-digit hex suffix for alpha opacity like `#aabbcc22`), add a brief inline comment explaining the encoding so future readers do not have to decode it.

On framework-specific documentation pages, verify that all prose references to the framework name (builder, renderer, etc.) match the page's actual subject. Copy-pasting from a sibling page commonly introduces incorrect framework name references.

The opening sentence of the Install section in `docs/get-started/frameworks/*.mdx` pages should follow the canonical phrasing: "To install Storybook in an existing [Framework] project, run this command in your project's root directory."

When editing framework documentation pages, check for and remove any content—migration callouts, configuration notes, or version-specific guidance—that applies only to Storybook major versions that are no longer supported or relevant to current users.

Keep PRs strictly scoped to their stated objective. Verify that every changed file is traceable to the PR's purpose; flag any unrelated changes and request extraction into a separate, focused pull request with its own description, tests, and documentation. In dependency-upgrade PRs specifically, flag any source or configuration changes that go beyond package manifest updates and mechanical API-migration fixes (e.g., renamed types, updated call signatures); ask the author to confirm each such change is intentional and explain why it is part of the upgrade.

In Vitest test files, place `vi.mock(...)` calls at the top of the file (outside any `describe` or `test` blocks) so Vitest's automatic hoisting works correctly. Configure mock return values and implementations (`vi.mocked(...)`, `vi.spyOn(...)`, `mockImplementationOnce`, `mockResolvedValueOnce`, etc.) in `beforeEach` blocks rather than inline within individual `it`/`test` bodies. Use nested `describe` blocks to scope test-specific configurations. Call `vi.clearAllMocks()` in `beforeEach` or `afterEach` to prevent cross-test state leakage. Avoid inline factory functions that re-implement module behavior; prefer the project's spy-mocking convention (see `.cursor/rules/spy-mocking.mdc`). Never manually reset mock state at the end of a test case; rely on `vi.clearAllMocks()` or `vi.resetAllMocks()` in `beforeEach`.

When adding non-obvious filtering or defensive logic that compensates for stale persisted state (e.g., `shortcutKeys` entries from localStorage never registered in the current session), include an inline comment explaining *why* the filtering is required—not just what it does.

Add JSDoc (`/** */` block comments, not `/* */`) to every exported utility function in framework, shared, and preset packages (e.g., under `code/frameworks/`, `code/core/`), including `internal_*` and `experimental_*` preset API functions. Document each function's purpose, each parameter, the full range of return values—including graceful-failure paths (e.g., 'returns `false` when the version string cannot be coerced by semver')—and stability status for preset APIs. For exported utilities consumed by packages outside their own module (e.g., called by builders or framework integrations), name those known consumers in the JSDoc so future readers can quickly understand the function's call sites without grepping the monorepo. Use `/** */` syntax so IDE hover tooltips are populated. Mark deprecated exports with the `@deprecated` JSDoc tag naming the replacement, e.g., `@deprecated Use api.getStoryHrefs from storybook/manager-api`. When types or interfaces in `scripts/ci/` map directly to external framework constructs (e.g., CircleCI step types, executor shapes), include a link to the relevant official documentation in the JSDoc description. When adding JSDoc to typed properties, ensure the comment provides information beyond what the type signature already encodes; comments that merely restate union variants or optional markers add noise and should be omitted or replaced with genuinely additive documentation.

When an API's configuration already constrains its callback arguments (e.g., `MutationObserver` with `attributeFilter`, or a typed event handler), do not add redundant `forEach` loops, `if` checks, or other guards that re-verify the guaranteed constraint; the extra code adds noise without safety.

Add explanatory inline or JSDoc comments to code that implements non-obvious workarounds (e.g., browser quirks, framework-specific issues like React.StrictMode, cross-frame communication, tooling constraints such as esbuild not supporting glob imports with query suffixes). The comment should describe the problem being solved, the specific runtime conditions or environment under which it occurs, and where applicable link to the relevant spec issue or browser bug, so future maintainers can reason about scope and continued necessity.

Reference shared internal constants (e.g., channel event names from `storybook/internal/core-events`, `STORYBOOK_FN_PLACEHOLDER`) by their exported named identifier everywhere they appear—production code, test assertions, and JSDoc comments—rather than hardcoding their string value. Never use inline magic strings for event names in `emit`/`on` calls.

Name event constants (e.g., in `core-events`) after the semantic purpose or behavioral contract they establish for consumers—what they should do or what state has changed—rather than the low-level browser mechanism that triggers them (e.g., prefer `FOCUS_TRAP_CHANGE` over `INERT_ATTRIBUTE_CHANGED`).

When editing MIGRATION.md, verify that no explanatory paragraph or sentence is accidentally duplicated within or across sections; each breaking-change or deprecation notice should appear exactly once.

When documenting or writing `yarn task` commands (in READMEs, instructions, AI-assistant guidance, etc.), always include the `--start-from` flag (e.g., `--start-from auto`) to prevent the CLI from entering interactive mode and blocking in non-interactive contexts such as CI or agent sessions. Use `yarn task` as the primary documented command form (the project's canonical task-runner wrapper); if raw `yarn nx` equivalents are shown, present them as alternatives alongside the `yarn task` form.

When attaching module-private metadata to objects (e.g., indentation style on a parsed `package.json`), define a module-level `Symbol('description')` constant (not `Symbol.for()`, which creates globally-shared symbols) and use it as the property key. Compute and attach such metadata at parse/load time so downstream writers can access it without a redundant file read. Add a brief inline comment noting that `JSON.stringify` silently omits symbol-keyed properties, as this serialization behavior is not universally known.

Avoid combining an existence check with a side-effecting operation in a single conditional expression. Separate them into distinct statements—first check, then act—so each step is independently readable and the side effect cannot be accidentally triggered as part of predicate evaluation.

When writing a comment that explains why an error is suppressed or treated as non-fatal, name the exact error type (e.g., `AbortError`) rather than using vague language like 'any errors' with a parenthetical example. Precision helps future maintainers know whether new error types should also be covered.

When introducing a custom helper type in a documentation snippet (e.g., under `docs/_snippets/`, to extend component props with additional story args), add a short comment directly above the type explaining its purpose and clearly stating whether it is optional for readers implementing the pattern in their own code.

When adding a callout or warning about a cross-cutting behavior (e.g., a builder quirk that affects build output), verify the note appears on every related documentation page—both the configuration API reference page and the corresponding integration or how-to guide—so the caveat is not buried in only one location.

When Storybook documentation recommends setting a Vite configuration option, specify that the setting must be applied through the `viteFinal` hook in `.storybook/main.ts` rather than referencing the Vite option in isolation; include an inline code snippet (e.g., `async viteFinal(config) { config.publicDir = false; return config; }`) or a link to Storybook's Vite builder documentation so readers know exactly where and how to apply the change.

When a utility is copied into a package because the original cannot be imported across a package boundary (e.g., the preview-to-manager boundary in addon-docs), add a `/** */` JSDoc block on the copy that explains: why it is duplicated, how it differs from the canonical version (e.g., only returns a preview URL rather than `{ managerHref, previewHref }`), and where the canonical version lives.

When calling `stringify` from `picoquery` in manager-api or router code, align the serialization options with the canonical usage in `code/core/src/router/utils.ts` (at minimum `nesting: true` and `nestingSyntax: 'js'`); document any intentional deviation from those defaults.

Do not leave test cases permanently disabled with `test.skip()` without an accompanying tracking issue or TODO that includes a resolution plan; error and exception branches (e.g., catch blocks and cross-origin fallback paths) must have dedicated test coverage.

When extracting a component ID from a story ID, do not split on `'--'` manually (e.g., `storyId.split('--')[0]`). Check whether `storybook/internal/csf` already provides a helper for story/component ID manipulation and use it instead.

Storybook tag strings such as `'autodocs'`, `'test'`, `'dev'`, `'manifest'`, `'attached-mdx'`, `'unattached-mdx'`, `'play-fn'`, and `'test-fn'` must be referenced via the canonical `Tag` object (defined in `code/core/src/shared/constants/tags.ts`, re-exported from `storybook/internal/core-server` for server/node code and from `storybook/manager-api` for manager/browser code). Raw string literals for these values are not acceptable anywhere in the codebase, including renderer packages such as `code/renderers/react/`.

The following files are auto-generated and must not be manually edited—changes will be overwritten: (1) `code/core/src/manager/globals/exports.ts` is generated by `code/core/scripts/generate-source-files.ts`; run the generator to discover new exports. (2) The rules table in `docs/configure/integration/eslint-plugin.mdx` is generated from per-rule markdown files under `code/lib/eslint-plugin/docs/rules/`; edit the source markdown to update rule descriptions.

Avoid CSS selector overrides in a parent/wrapper styled component that target internals of a child component (e.g., `table { backgroundColor: ... }` inside a wrapper div). Components should accept styling customization only through explicit APIs such as props or a `className` prop. If the child component lacks the necessary API for context-specific styling, extend the child component with that API rather than reaching into it with an ancestor selector. When a styling fix is correct for all usages of a component (not just one specific consumer), apply the change in the component's own definition rather than as a context-specific override in a single consumer.

When adding or modifying entries in `sandbox-templates.ts` to enable a Storybook configuration option for CI coverage, check whether the option is supported by both Webpack and Vite builders; if it is, add sandbox entries for both builder types rather than only one. When setting a modification flag on a sandbox template (e.g., `useCsfFactory: true`), apply the same flag to all builder variants (Vite, Webpack, RsBuild) of the same renderer unless there is a documented technical reason they must differ. If only one builder supports the option, add a comment explaining why the other is omitted.

When rendering a Radix-UI–style polymorphic component (such as `ActionList.Action`) as an anchor element, use the `asChild` pattern—pass an `<a>` element as a JSX child—rather than supplying an `as='a'` prop. This is the established polymorphism convention throughout this codebase.

When adding a new feature flag to the `StorybookConfigRaw` features interface (in `code/core/src/types/modules/core-common.ts`), choose user-facing, discoverable names rather than internal technical jargon. Prefer terminology users are likely to search for in documentation (e.g., 'onboarding') and include a surface-area scope prefix (e.g., 'sidebar') when the flag controls behaviour in a specific part of the UI. The flag name, its default in the preset (`common-preset.ts`), and all usage sites must all use the same identifier.

Preset hook functions intended solely for internal Storybook-to-Storybook consumption must use the `internal_` prefix (e.g., `internal_getArgTypesData`); reserve the `experimental_` prefix for APIs that are deliberately surfaced to end users.

Preset hook functions should follow the chainable accumulator pattern `(input: T, options: Options) => T` so they compose correctly in preset chains; if an internal hook must have a different input/output shape, document the deviation explicitly.

Renderer-specific preset hook functions that require file-system access should use async FS APIs and be declared `async`; since `core-server` will consume these hooks uniformly across all renderers, an async contract must be established from the start to keep the API consistent.

Do not create two near-identical utility modules that differ only in naming conventions or minor constant values; consolidate them into a single canonical implementation with a clear name and update all call sites, to prevent the two copies from diverging silently.

When adding a new `SBType` variant whose properties must be extensible across multiple renderers or frameworks (e.g., `renderer`), type the property as the open `string` type rather than a closed string-literal union, so new renderers can be integrated without requiring changes to the type definition itself.

Vitest/Jest `describe` block titles must exactly match the name of the function, class, or module under test; stale or incorrect titles produce misleading test-runner output and make failures hard to trace. Similarly, `it()` and `test()` description strings must accurately reflect the actual behavior, return value, and type being asserted—do not use terminology from unrelated type shapes or describe a different scenario than what the test actually verifies.

Debug log messages must accurately describe and reference the variable actually being logged; if the intent is to log a count or derived value, name it correctly in the message string and pass the right variable. Error return payloads should include the actual captured error message rather than a generic fixed string like `'Failed to find candidates'`.

When a refactor makes existing code paths unnecessary—unused imports, intermediate renamed variables, derived variables, or utility functions no longer called—delete all dead code in the same PR. Stale imports create false dependency signals and will trigger lint/compiler warnings; leftover dead variables and functions add noise and confuse future readers.

Do not declare props in a styled component's generic type parameter unless the styling function actually reads and applies them. A prop like `muted?: boolean` that is declared but never used in the styles creates dead API surface: callers pass it expecting an effect, but nothing happens. Either wire the prop into the style logic or remove it from the type.

When replacing a bespoke styled component with a shared design-system component, visually verify in stories that all interactive states (focus ring offset, hover background, active color) still match the surrounding UI. Shared components may default to a different `outline-offset`, `border-radius`, or `background` than what was previously hardcoded, causing subtle visual regressions.

Render purely decorative characters (colons, slashes, separators) via CSS `content` on a `::before`/`::after` pseudo-element rather than as HTML text nodes. Text-node decorators are announced by screen readers and braille displays, adding noise without conveying meaning.

Name component props after what the data semantically *is* (e.g., `aside`, `extra`, `secondary`) rather than where it visually *appears* (e.g., `right`, `trailing`, `end`). Visual layout can change across redesigns, but the underlying data model should not; positional names become misleading after any layout change.
